cues.text: Another Imperial Schism
The papacy of Alexander III was contested from its earliest days by Emperor Frederick Barbarossa .
Frederick backed four antipopes in rapid succession over nearly two decades, seeking to bend the papacy to imperial will and reassert control over church appointments.
The Concordat of Worms had supposedly settled that issue a generation earlier.

Alexander spent long years in exile from Rome, at times finding refuge in France, sustained by the support of the French and English crowns and the emerging Lombard League of northern Italian cities that resisted Frederick's ambitions in Italy.
The deadlock broke in 1176, when Lombard forces defeated Frederick decisively at the Battle of Legnano , a rare instance of a medieval urban militia defeating an imperial army in open battle.
The following year, emperor and pope met at Venice and formally reconciled in a ceremony rich with symbolic submission.
This ended the schism, clearing the way for Alexander to summon a general council to close the affair and address a broader agenda of reform.
The Council of 1179
The council opened at the Lateran in March 1179 with roughly three hundred bishops present from across Latin Christendom, along with representatives of the reconciled emperor.
Alexander III had weathered nearly two decades of schism and exile, one of the longest and most difficult pontificates of the medieval period.
He presided over an assembly determined to prevent any recurrence of the disputed elections that had produced rival popes throughout his pontificate.
Its most consequential decision addressed exactly that problem at its root.
Reforming Papal Elections
Canon 1 of the council decreed that a valid papal election required a two-thirds majority of the cardinals.
This rule was designed to make it far harder for a minority faction to produce a rival claimant, as Anacletus II and Frederick's antipopes had done.

This provision, with later refinements, remains the foundation of papal election procedure to the present day, making Third Lateran's single most cited legacy a rule of Church governance rather than a doctrinal definition.
The council also set a minimum age of thirty for the office of bishop and renewed strictures against simony in ecclesiastical appointments.
Confronting Heresy and Reforming Morals
The council also addressed heretical movements spreading in southern France and northern Italy, condemning the Cathars (also called Albigensians) and the Waldensians .
It called on secular rulers to assist in suppressing them—an early step toward the Albigensian Crusade, which would come a generation later.

Other canons addressed usury, protections for crusaders, and the pastoral care of lepers, ordering that leper communities be permitted their own churches, cemeteries, and priests separate from the wider parish.

Taken together, the council's canons reflect a Church newly confident after its long constitutional struggle with the empire, turning its energy toward internal reform and the emerging challenge of organized doctrinal dissent.
Legacy

Third Lateran's two-thirds rule for papal elections proved to be one of the most durable pieces of legislation produced by any medieval council, still governing papal conclaves in modified form today.
Its early, still relatively measured response to Catharism and Waldensianism also marks an important staging point.
It marks the Church's escalating engagement with medieval heresy, a concern that would grow far more urgent — and far more severe in its methods — over the following decades.
